article.title: Improve Data Integrity
article.author: Britta Hedlund
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Every report, invoice, and forecast a business produces is only as reliable as the data underneath it. When that data is wrong, the damage spreads quietly. Balances drift, orders lose their invoices, and teams start keeping their own spreadsheets because they no longer trust the system. For organizations running ASE, Sybase consulting experts help restore that trust by improving two things at once: the accuracy of stored data and the reliability of every transaction that changes it. Both sound technical, and in part they are. But the payoff is entirely practical. Finance closes the month without reconciliation headaches, customers see correct balances, and auditors find records that agree with each other. Two Goals That Depend on Each Other Data integrity and transaction consistency are closely related, yet they protect against different problems. The table below shows how they differ. Problems in one area often look like problems in the other, which is why tracing them takes experience. Many businesses bring in Sybase consulting experts once doubts about their data appear, because finding where an error started is usually harder than fixing it. How Consultants Improve Data Integrity 1. Measuring the Current State The work starts with facts rather than assumptions. Consultants run health checks on the database, look for duplicate and orphaned records, and compare key totals between ASE and the systems that rely on it. The result is a clear list of problems ranked by business impact, so effort goes where it matters most. This step often reveals that a handful of tables cause most of the trouble. A single customer table with duplicate entries, for example, can ripple into billing, reporting, and support systems at once. Fixing that one source usually does more good than chasing hundreds of individual errors downstream. 2. Building Business Rules Into the Database In many older systems, the rules that keep data clean live only inside application code. That works until a second application, a bulk import, or a quick script writes to the same tables without those checks. Consultants move the essential rules into the database itself. Keys stop duplicates, relationships between tables prevent orphaned records, and value checks keep entries within sensible limits. Once the database enforces these rules, every program has to follow them. 3. Cleaning Existing Data Safely New rules can't be switched on while bad data is still sitting in the tables. Consultants work with business owners to agree how each type of error should be corrected, then clean the data in small, controlled batches. This avoids disrupting daily operations and leaves a clear record of what changed. 4. Catching Damage Before It Spreads Storage problems can sit unnoticed for months while the server keeps running normally. Consultants set up regular integrity checks using ASE's built-in dbcc tools and make sure someone reviews the results. Catching a damaged page early turns a potential crisis into routine maintenance. How Consultants Improve Transaction Consistency 1. Making Every Change All or Nothing A transaction should either complete fully or leave no trace. In ASE, though, many errors stop only the current statement and let the rest of the transaction continue. Unless the code checks for that, part of the work can be saved while the rest is lost. Consultants review stored procedures and application code so every failure triggers a proper rollback. This one improvement often removes a whole category of puzzling partial updates. 2. Bringing Clarity to Transaction Settings ASE can start and end transactions in two different ways, and code written for one approach may behave unexpectedly under the other. Consultants document which approach each application uses and test against it. They also help teams choose how strictly transactions are isolated from one another, balancing accuracy against speed. 3. Keeping Copies of the Data in Sync Many ASE environments copy data to standby or reporting servers. Over time, those copies can drift because of one-sided manual fixes or errors during replication. Consultants compare the copies with the original on a regular schedule and correct whatever caused the gap, so every system reports the same numbers. 4. Making Recovery Accurate A backup restores whatever it captured, good or bad. Consultants make sure backups form an unbroken chain and that the database can be restored to a precise moment. That matters most when a faulty batch job needs to be undone, since the business can roll back to just before it ran instead of losing a full day of work. What Businesses Gain The improvements add up to something simple: data people can rely on. Finance teams spend less time reconciling figures, support teams stop running manual correction scripts, and audits go faster because records agree across systems. Just as important, a clean and well-documented database is far easier to upgrade or migrate later, including a move to SQL Server. There's a quieter benefit too. When people trust the system, they stop building workarounds around it. The side spreadsheets, manual checks, and duplicate reports that grew up to compensate for unreliable data can finally be retired, which saves time across every team that touches the numbers. Frequently Asked Questions What's the difference between data integrity and transaction consistency? Integrity is about whether stored data is correct and undamaged. Consistency is about whether each transaction leaves the database in a valid state. A business needs both to trust its numbers. Will adding database rules slow down applications? There's a small overhead when data is inserted or updated, but it's usually minor compared with the cost of cleaning up bad data later. Good indexing keeps the impact low. Can a faulty batch job be undone in ASE? Yes, if transaction log backups are complete. The database can be restored and rolled forward to just before the job ran, which is why an unbroken backup chain matters so much. Final Perspective Reliable data doesn't come from a single fix. It comes from rules the database enforces, storage that's checked regularly, transactions that complete fully or not at all, and recovery plans that have been tested. Sybase consulting experts strengthen each of these areas, so the figures a business depends on are figures it can trust.
